incidentPremise: The night supervisor reported 'a man standing at the end of aisle B' four times in one shift and walked the aisle four times to find nothing. On the fifth call she stopped walking and watched the camera instead, and it was still there. She kept the feed up for six hours until the shift ended, and it did not move once. It has been eleven days.
_designNote:
The SECOND incident package for this map, and it exists to prove the engine is content rather than one anomaly (GDD 15, 26.2 — three packages testing distinct procedure families). It shares the cold store, the equipment manifest and the evidence ledger with the graybox-draught, and it plays nothing like it.

The draught is a HEAT problem: you build a wall out of a field and it cannot cross. This is an OBSERVATION problem: it does not move while anyone is looking at it, so the squad's resource is not heat but attention — and attention is the thing you run out of when you also have to carry, place, power and seal. The whole procedure is therefore about handing coverage from a person to a camera and back without ever dropping it.

It needs no new engine code beyond the two perception senses. There is no 'heat-wall' trigger in this file at all: enclosure is irrelevant to it, and the engine simply never evaluates a wildcard it was not given.

field._note: It is not a temperature. The thermal imager shows it as an ordinary room-temperature mass — which is precisely the false lead, because a squad that has read the draught's file arrives expecting the imager to be the answer and it tells them nothing at all.

perception.recordingInterference: None, and that is the point. It records perfectly. It is visible to the naked eye and to every camera; what it will not do is move while it is being recorded or watched. An anomaly that also corrupted its own recording would remove the only tool that works on it.
accessibilityAlternatives: Coverage is reported as a count and a named source ('held by camera 2'), never by colour alone.
The release warning is a sustained rising tone AND a caption AND the coverage count falling to zero, so it does not require hearing, colour vision, or reading fast.

states.description: Motionless at the end of an aisle. It has been there for eleven days. It does not react to being approached.

presentation.visualTell: A figure at the limit of the light, facing away, at the wrong scale for the distance
presentation.audioCue: Nothing at all. The room noise drops out around it, which is itself the cue
presentation.environmentalTell: Dust does not settle within about a metre of it

states.description: Unobserved, it closes. Fast, in a straight line, and it stops the instant anything sees it again.

presentation.visualTell: It is nearer than it was, in a posture nobody watched it take
presentation.audioCue: A single footfall's worth of sound, arriving after it has already stopped
presentation.environmentalTell: Loose paper lifts in its wake

states.description: Under continuous observation. It cannot move and it cannot act. This is not a weakness the squad found; it is the only reason anyone survived the eleven days.

presentation.visualTell: Perfectly still, in whatever posture it was caught in
presentation.environmentalTell: Dust begins to settle on it

states.description: Inside a sealed transit case with its interior camera running and recording to two separate stores. Custody is the camera, not the box.

presentation.visualTell: Case-mounted indicator steady; the interior feed shows it exactly as it was sealed
presentation.audioCue: Recorder cycling, roughly every twenty seconds

_latencyNote: ⚠ THE OBSERVATION TRIGGERS TOLERATE 900ms AND THEY USED TO TOLERATE 300. §8.2 requires every rule to be fair under latency, and this is the anomaly where that costs the most: whether it is being watched is decided by where five people are looking, and a client's report of where it is looking is exactly the thing a bad wire delays. Section AM models a worst wire of 250ms of latency plus 200ms of jitter, and at 300ms these two rules could have been decided by the network rather than by the squad — the figure moving because a snapshot was late, on the one anomaly whose whole rule is that it does not move while you look at it. Nothing in the world is slower for it; the sustains in the content are unchanged. What changed is how much wire the rule survives.

triggers.condition: at least one operative or powered remote camera has it in view, unobstructed
triggers.telegraph: It stops mid-stride, without decelerating, the instant coverage is established.

triggers.condition: no operative and no powered camera has held it in view for longer than 1.5s
triggers.telegraph: The room noise drops away about three quarters of a second before it moves — the only warning, and it is the same one the night supervisor described.

triggers.condition: a warm body within 9m for longer than 3s, while nothing is watching it
triggers.telegraph: The dust stops settling. Nothing else changes.

triggers.condition: transit case closed around it while it is under observation, interior camera live
triggers.telegraph: The lid comes over and the interior feed picks it up before the daylight goes.

capabilities.effect: It arrives at arm's length and takes hold. Serious mobility injury and cognitive stress; survivable once, and nobody has been recorded surviving it twice.
Powered equipment within range browns out while it is moving. A camera that dies is a camera that stops holding it, which is the trap: the fence you built is also the thing it eats.

constraints.description: It cannot move while observed. Any single unobstructed viewer is enough — a person, a deployed remote camera, it does not distinguish. This is the whole procedure: the squad does not fence it, they never stop looking at it.

Observation is geometric. Racking, panel walls and closed doors break it, and the aisles are long straight runs — which is why coverage in this building is a matter of standing in the right place rather than owning enough cameras.

Darkness is irrelevant to it and to the cameras' ability to hold it. Restoring the mains helps the squad see each other and nothing else. A team that spends its whole operation on the breakers has solved the previous incident, not this one.

_evidenceNote:
Four second paths, one per required rule (GDD §27.2, added at revision 0.2.0). The list is read in PAIRS and each pair is two different kinds of observation.

The hard part here is that `seen` and `unwatched` are the same coin, so a careless second path for one is a restatement of the other. They are split on what the observation RECORDS rather than on what it means: `seen` is evidenced by things that STOPPED — a woman who watched for six hours, and drag marks with no taper at either end — while `unwatched` is evidenced by things that CHANGED BETWEEN TWO LOOKS: eleven days of footage in which it is never caught moving, and five phone calls giving four different positions inside forty-six minutes.

`unwatched` is the only rule here whose first path costs cargo, so its second is the switchboard log, which is free and lies on the way in. The forklift driver is graded disputed on purpose: he is one frightened man who did it twice, and §7.3 has a word for that rather than a reason to leave him out.

evidenceRules.rawObservation: Night supervisor states she called it in four times and walked the aisle four times, and on the fifth she watched the camera instead and it stayed. She says she did not blink for six hours, which is not possible, and she says it anyway.

Drag marks in eleven days of dust down aisle B: five runs of three to four metres each, laid end to end along the lane. Every one of them begins and ends square, with no taper at either end and no scuffing out to the sides.
Eleven days of recorded footage. In every frame in which it appears it is stationary. Every change of position falls in a gap between recordings, or behind a passing shelf.

Site switchboard log for that night. Five calls from the storage extension between 01:12 and 01:58, each written up with the position the caller gave: end of aisle B, end of aisle B, halfway down aisle B, end of aisle B, and against the mesh by the door. Nothing after 01:58, and the shift ran to 06:00.
A circle of bare floor roughly one metre across where dust has not settled, in a room that has been shut for eleven days.

Day-shift forklift driver. He states he has taken aisle B twice since and both times stopped at the pallet line and sent his mate down instead. He says the once he went past the line himself it was nearer when he came back out, and that he was down there 'about a five-count'.
Site electrical log shows fourteen unexplained brownouts on the storage circuit, none of them matching a load event, all of them under nine seconds.
Both emergency luminaires on this floor are showing a fault LED. The counter behind each diffuser — one count for every supply dropout the fitting has carried — reads 14 on one and 13 on the other.
Thermal imager reads it at ambient, to within the instrument's error. It is exactly as warm as the wall behind it.
Roster shows the same three names on every night shift for two years. One of them stopped signing in eleven days ago and was not reported absent.

containment.goal: The figure sealed inside a transit case with its interior camera live and recording, verified by thirty seconds of continuous interior coverage. Custody is the camera. A case with a dead recorder is a box with something in it.

abortConditions: Coverage falls to zero at any point after it has begun closing
Any operative takes a second contact
A camera holding it browns out with no second viewer covering the same lane
Coverage depends on one viewer for longer than 10s
Power pack drops below the reserve needed to carry the cameras through the seal
Dust sample taken from the ring is compromised before the case is sealed
Any condition from the safe procedure

integrityConditions.failureSignal: The interior feed drops to static, and the case gets appreciably heavier.
The coverage count falls to one, and the room noise thins.
A camera indicator dips amber a second or so before the feed goes.
